pages.text: It was harmattan in Tamale. The wind blew dry and dusty from the Sahara, the sun looked like a pale orange coin, and every surface wore a thin layer of dust. At the boarding school, evening study was almost over when Fuseini gasped. “Look at the field.”
sentences: It was harmattan in Tamale.
The wind blew dry and dusty from the Sahara, the sun looked like a pale orange coin, and every surface wore a thin layer of dust.
At the boarding school, evening study was almost over when Fuseini gasped.
“Look at the field.”
pages.alt: A dusty school field at dusk with a pale orange sun behind a haze.

pages.text: A pale figure stood in the middle of the field, tall and thin, swaying. It slowly turned. Students at the windows whispered. “A ghost,” said one. “The dust spirit,” said another. Zubeida, who could always hear the wind, felt it humming in her ears. “It is not angry,” she said. “It is… asking.”
sentences: A pale figure stood in the middle of the field, tall and thin, swaying.
It slowly turned.
Students at the windows whispered.
“A ghost,” said one.
“The dust spirit,” said another.
Zubeida, who could always hear the wind, felt it humming in her ears.
“It is not angry,” she said.
“It is… asking.”
pages.alt: Students at a window point at a pale swirling figure on the dusty field.

pages.text: Mr Wumbei, the science teacher, came out with a clipboard. “Let us be careful,” he said. “Not frightened, not foolish.” Fuseini brought a thermometer. Zubeida held up a strip of cloth. “First,” said Mr Wumbei, “observe from a distance, then test.”
sentences: Mr Wumbei, the science teacher, came out with a clipboard.
“Let us be careful,” he said.
“Not frightened, not foolish.” Fuseini brought a thermometer.
Zubeida held up a strip of cloth.
“First,” said Mr Wumbei, “observe from a distance, then test.”
pages.alt: A teacher and two students stand on the school steps with a thermometer and a cloth strip.

pages.text: Fuseini read the thermometer: the bare ground was much hotter than the air above it. “Hot ground heats the air just above it,” he said. “The hot air rises quickly in a column.” The figure grew taller, and its base spun faster. “That could pull dust into a spinning column,” he said. “A dust devil.”
sentences: Fuseini read the thermometer: the bare ground was much hotter than the air above it.
“Hot ground heats the air just above it,” he said.
“The hot air rises quickly in a column.” The figure grew taller, and its base spun faster.
“That could pull dust into a spinning column,” he said.
“A dust devil.”
pages.alt: A student reads a thermometer near the baked ground while a dust column rises behind him.

pages.text: Behind them, in the hostel, two students laughed and shook a nylon blanket in the dark. Blue sparks crackled along it. “Ghost lightning!” cried a girl. “It is static electricity,” said Fuseini. “Very dry air lets charge build up on cloth.” Mr Wumbei nodded. “Harmattan air is very dry, so it happens often.”
sentences: Behind them, in the hostel, two students laughed and shook a nylon blanket in the dark.
Blue sparks crackled along it.
“Ghost lightning!” cried a girl.
“It is static electricity,” said Fuseini.
“Very dry air lets charge build up on cloth.” Mr Wumbei nodded.
“Harmattan air is very dry, so it happens often.”
pages.alt: Students in a dark room shake a blanket that gives off tiny blue sparks.

pages.text: Out on the field, the dust devil lurched towards the school. “Back inside, everyone!” called Mr Wumbei. “Cover your eyes and mouth. Never walk into a dust devil.” Students hurried in and shut the windows. Zubeida stayed at the door, her hair whipping. “Wait,” she whispered to the wind. “Please.”
sentences: Out on the field, the dust devil lurched towards the school.
“Back inside, everyone!” called Mr Wumbei.
“Cover your eyes and mouth.
Never walk into a dust devil.” Students hurried in and shut the windows.
Zubeida stayed at the door, her hair whipping.
“Wait,” she whispered to the wind.
“Please.”
pages.alt: A swirling dust column moves across the field as students run inside and a girl stands at the door.

pages.text: Zubeida began to hum a low, steady note. The whirl slowed. For a moment, the dust column seemed to turn its head, like a listener. Then it bent away from the school, drifted to the empty field edge, spread out, and sank into a gentle swirl of dust on the ground.
sentences: Zubeida began to hum a low, steady note.
The whirl slowed.
For a moment, the dust column seemed to turn its head, like a listener.
Then it bent away from the school, drifted to the empty field edge, spread out, and sank into a gentle swirl of dust on the ground.
pages.alt: A girl hums at the doorway as the dust column bends away and settles on the far edge of the field.

pages.text: Silence. The sun slipped away. “Did you do that?” asked Fuseini. “Or did it just fade?” Zubeida smiled. “Dust devils do die out, and the wind changes.” “But?” “But it listened,” she said. Mr Wumbei wrote in his notes: Observed. Explained. Safe. And one line more: Do not rule out wonder. The end.
sentences: Silence.
The sun slipped away.
“Did you do that?” asked Fuseini.
“Or did it just fade?” Zubeida smiled.
“Dust devils do die out, and the wind changes.” “But?” “But it listened,” she said.
Mr Wumbei wrote in his notes: Observed.
Explained.
Safe.
And one line more: Do not rule out wonder.
The end.
pages.alt: A girl, a boy and a teacher stand together at dusk as the last dust settles on the field.

activities.question: What did Fuseini say causes a dust devil?
options: Hot ground heating air that rises in a spinning column

activities.question: What explains the sparks on the nylon blanket?
options: Static electricity in very dry air

activities.prompt: The dust devil is moving towards the school. What is the safest thing for the students to do?
options: Go inside, close windows and cover eyes and mouth
Stand in the doorway to watch

activities.definition: A dry, dusty wind that blows from the Sahara over West Africa, mostly between about November and March.

items: Students saw a pale figure on the field.
The dust devil moved towards the school.
Everyone went inside and the whirl faded away.

activities.prompt: Zubeida felt something she could not explain, and still stayed careful. How do you feel about things science cannot yet explain?

glossary.definition: A dry, dusty wind from the Sahara that blows across West Africa in the dry season.
A build-up of electric charge on things that are rubbed together, often in dry air.
A tall, thin shape like a pillar.
Look carefully and notice what is happening.
